title: Short Stuff: The Return of Bill Gates!
summary: Short Stuff episode featuring an interview with Bill Gates about COVID-19 vaccines and therapeutics. Gates discusses the range of vaccine candidates and what trials must measure (transmission blocking, preventing illness, efficacy in the elderly, duration, cost); why affordability matters more than efficacy for low-income countries; tiered pricing and the Gavi-style global access effort (the transcript renders it as "gobby"); the RNA (mRNA) vaccine approach and its lipid packaging cost; manufacturing partnerships with Serum Institute and Biological E in India; why the economic case for COVID vaccines is stronger than for diseases like malaria and TB; flu vaccine limitations versus COVID; therapeutics such as remdesivir and dexamethasone plus monoclonal antibodies; bat exposure and surveillance for future spillover; US funding for global health; Gates's philanthropic shift and child mortality; and remote work during lockdown. The episode closes with a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening and introduction of Bill Gates
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and guest Bill Gates, saying the conversation will cover COVID-19, vaccines and therapeutics.

segments.title: Vaccine candidates and what makes a good vaccine
segments.summary: Gates describes the range of COVID-19 vaccine candidates and the properties being tested: transmission blocking, preventing illness, efficacy in elderly people, duration and cost. He names candidates expected to come out first and says affordability matters as much as efficacy.

segments.title: Multiple vaccines, herd immunity and the scale of doses
segments.summary: Discussion of whether families will need to choose between vaccines, how natural immunity and vaccination combine for herd immunity, and the two-dose requirement that means roughly 140 million doses for the US population of about 70 million vaccinated people.

segments.title: Tiered pricing and access in low and middle income countries
segments.summary: Gates explains that manufacturers agreed to price vaccines for the poorest countries near marginal cost, with tiered pricing, and estimates some constructs at about two dollars per dose. He describes the Gavi-linked purchasing effort and the RNA vaccine's higher costs.

segments.title: RNA vaccines and how they work
segments.summary: Gates explains that RNA vaccines send instructions telling cells to make a protein, so less material is needed, though packaging the RNA in lipids adds cost. He notes Moderna and BioNTech were founded around this approach and that it could be important for future vaccines.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts announce a short break before returning to Gates.

segments.title: International manufacturing partnerships and research cooperation
segments.summary: Gates describes unusual cooperation among governments and companies, including licensing arrangements that let other companies, including Serum Institute of India and Biological E, manufacture vaccines at scale. He says few people are being greedy.

segments.title: Economics of pandemic vaccines versus diseases of poor countries
segments.summary: Gates argues the economic cost of COVID-19 gives a strong market signal, unlike tuberculosis or malaria, which mostly affect poor countries and have weak market incentives. He mentions US relief spending.

segments.title: Vaccine hesitancy and why flu vaccines differ
segments.summary: Josh raises vaccine wariness and the question of whether COVID vaccines will work when flu shots sometimes fail. Gates explains flu vaccine limits: many circulating strains, strain-selection misses, and weak protection in elderly people. He says the coronavirus has minimal genetic variation.

segments.title: COVID-19 therapeutics
segments.summary: Gates says doctors treat COVID-19 better than at the start, using less ventilation and earlier oxygen and steroids. He names remdesivir and dexamethasone, oral antivirals, and monoclonal antibodies from Regeneron, Eli Lilly and AstraZeneca, and predicts the death rate could fall substantially before vaccines are widely deployed.

segments.title: Life after vaccines, reservoirs and global equity
segments.summary: Gates discusses what the world looks like once vaccines and treatments are available, including eradication and surveillance. He discusses US funding for global health, past efforts on smallpox and polio, and the argument for helping other countries. He also mentions Australia and South Korea.
topics: Australia and South Korea COVID response

segments.title: Bats, live markets and future spillover prevention
segments.summary: Gates discusses bat coronaviruses south of Wuhan, the likely crossover at live markets, cross-protection and Vietnam's response, and the need for reduced bat exposure, strong surveillance and rapid large-scale testing.

segments.title: Gates's philanthropy and child mortality
segments.summary: Gates explains how he and Melinda shifted from Microsoft work to global health after learning that vaccines for childhood diseases were unaffordable for poor countries. He cites child under-five mortality falling from about ten percent to about five percent and the goal of reducing it further.

segments.title: Remote work, family life and reading
segments.summary: Gates describes lockdown family time, feedback to Microsoft on remote collaboration tools, reduced business travel, and a book by Zeke Emmanuel on health systems.

segments.title: Wrap-up and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Gates, mention a Stuff You Should Know board game, and close the Short Stuff episode.
